extracted.intended_audience: educational institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, campus legal counsel, and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX nondisclosure and informal resolution
extracted.subtask_description: Implementation and application guidance for §106.44(j) (nondisclosure of personally identifiable information) and §106.44(k) (informal resolution) of the Department of Education's Title IX regulations, including permitted exceptions, limits, timing, and required safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disclosure of personally identifiable information obtained in course of complying with Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may not disclose any personally identifiable information obtained by the recipient in the course of complying with this part unless consent is obtained or one of the enumerated exceptions applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition applies broadly (includes information about supportive measures, requests for reasonable modification, complainants, respondents, witnesses, and other participants in informal resolution, grievance procedures, and, if applicable, §106.46). The Department adopted this prohibition to avoid chilling reporting and to prevent sex-based harm (harassment, retaliation, discrimination) resulting from unauthorized disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the term 'personally identifiable information' rather than 'identity'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adopted the phrase 'personally identifiable information' in final §106.44(j) rather than 'identity'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chosen term is more comprehensive than 'identity' because it covers information that would tend to reveal an individual's identity (not merely a name). The Department did not adopt a narrow statutory definition here because recipients are generally familiar with the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of PII protection — covered persons and contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The nondisclosure paragraph covers personally identifiable information obtained with regard to complainants, respondents, witnesses, advisors, parents, guardians, other authorized representatives, interpreters, notetakers, and other participants in Title IX procedures, including informal resolution and grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: information about supportive measures or requests for pregnancy-related reasonable modifications (§106.40(b)(3)) is protected. The rule is intended to prevent unnecessary disclosures that could chill participation or cause harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception (j)(1): Prior written consent from a person with legal right to consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(1) permits disclosure when the recipient has obtained prior written consent to the disclosure from a person with the legal right to consent to the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must obtain consent from the person who has legal authority under applicable Federal and State law; that person may not be the same as the person whose PII is at issue (e.g., a parent for a minor). If the PII is in an education record, FERPA consent requirements apply. State law may govern consent when PII is not in an education record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception (j)(2): Disclosures to parents/guardians/authorized legal representatives with legal right
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(2) clarifies that the nondisclosure paragraph does not prohibit disclosure to a parent, guardian, or other authorized legal representative who has the legal right to receive disclosures on behalf of the person whose PII is at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception is intended to allow application of legal rights from other Federal laws (e.g., FERPA) and State laws. Example: parents of elementary/secondary students generally have FERPA rights to inspect education records; FERPA may limit disclosures to parents of postsecondary 'eligible students' absent consent or a FERPA exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception (j)(3): Disclosures to carry out the purposes of Title IX regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(3) permits disclosures necessary to carry out the purposes of the Department's Title IX regulations, including action taken to address conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination in the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in postsecondary contexts a recipient may inform a professor of a supportive measure needed for classroom implementation but may not disclose unrelated complaint details. This exception allows disclosures required/permitted under §§106.44, 106.45, or 106.46, such as providing parties an equal opportunity to access relevant evidence (§106.45(f)(4); §106.46(e)(6)) or permitting advisors/others at meetings (§106.46(e)(3)), but such disclosures must not conflict with FERPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception (j)(4): Disclosures required by Federal law, Federal regulations, or terms of Federal awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(4) permits disclosures that are required by Federal law, Federal regulations, or the terms and conditions of a Federal award (including grant awards or funding agreements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department added this to clarify that such required disclosures are permissible, but they must also be consistent with FERPA. The provision also addresses interaction with statutes/regulations like HIPAA and clarifies the exception is focused on Federal law (State law addressed separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception (j)(5): Disclosures permitted or required by FERPA or State/local law to extent not in conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(5) allows disclosures that are permitted, but not required, under FERPA, and permits disclosures required by State or local law to the extent such disclosures do not conflict with Title IX or the Department's Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if FERPA or State/local law would allow a disclosure, a recipient may not make it if it would conflict with Title IX (e.g., cause sex-based discrimination, chill reporting, be retaliatory, or hinder the recipient's Title IX obligations). Example: FERPA may permit certain disclosures under 20 U.S.C. 1232g(b) or 34 CFR 99.31, but disclosures that create a hostile environment or are retaliatory remain prohibited. State/local laws that conflict with Title IX are preempted under §106.6(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disclosures for retaliatory purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when an exception applies, a disclosure cannot be made for retaliatory purposes per §106.71.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that disclosures made to punish, harass, or retaliate against the individual whose PII is at issue are forbidden. Disclosures that create a hostile environment (e.g., broad disclosure of a student's sexual orientation or gender identity leading to harassment) would be prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to ensure compatibility with FERPA and other applicable Federal law when disclosing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients making disclosures under any exception must ensure compliance with FERPA or any other applicable Federal laws and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, disclosures under Federal award terms must be consistent with FERPA; presence of advisors or sharing evidence must not conflict with FERPA. Recipients must verify legal authority before disclosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent access to complainant/witness identities is not unlimited
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents are not entitled to know the identity of all complainants, witnesses, and other participants without limitation; identity disclosures are governed by the regulations and due process needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department stresses its longstanding approach (including 2020 amendments) that anonymity is not guaranteed but disclosures are only permitted when due process necessitates it (see §106.44(j)(3) and discussion of §106.45(b)(5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution may be offered voluntarily and broadly (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(k) permits recipients to offer informal resolution processes (alternative dispute resolution) that are voluntary, informed, and may be offered without a formal complaint, at any time prior to determining whether sex discrimination occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution can encompass many conflict-resolution strategies and is intended to give recipients discretion to tailor responses. The Department retained the requirement that facilitators be appropriately trained (§106.8(d)(3)). However, informal resolution must not be offered in two situations: when there are allegations that an employee engaged in sex-based harassment of an elementary or secondary school student, or when the process would conflict with Federal, State, or local law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement for informal resolution facilitators
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person facilitating informal resolutions must be appropriately trained under §106.8(d)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'informal' is not meant to imply less robust training or independence; facilitators should have comparable preparation and independence as those involved in formal grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and withdrawal rights in informal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may participate in informal resolution before an investigation commences or during an investigation; any party has the right to withdraw from informal resolution prior to agreeing to a resolution and to initiate or resume the recipient's grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A determination whether sex discrimination occurred can only be made at the conclusion of grievance procedures (§106.45, and if applicable §106.46); an out-of-process admission alone is not a determination. If a party breaches a resolution agreement or the recipient discovers fraud, the recipient may void the agreement and initiate or resume grievance procedures, provided the recipient acts equitably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible contents/terms of informal resolution agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential terms of an informal resolution agreement may include, but are not limited to, restrictions on contact, restrictions on the respondent's participation in one or more of the recipient's programs or activities, or attendance at specific events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms may be similar to supportive measures, remedies, or disciplinary sanctions that a recipient could have imposed had it determined sex discrimination occurred under grievance procedures. §106.44(g)(2) does not prohibit terms that resemble supportive measures from being part of an informal resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion to decline informal resolution and factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient has discretion to decline to offer informal resolution (even with parties' consent) in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations meriting decline may include evidence of actual or potential coercion, ongoing threat to others, age-appropriateness concerns (especially in elementary/secondary settings), or other equitable considerations. The recipient may consider the factors enumerated in §106.44(f)(1)(v)(A) when deciding. Any decision to decline must be exercised in a manner equitable to the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution not available for complaints alleging discrimination by the recipient (structural complaints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal resolution is not available for complaints that do not involve a person (e.g., complaints that a recipient's policy or practice discriminates on the basis of sex), because those complaints allege discrimination by the recipient itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many cases a Title IX Coordinator can address potentially discriminatory policies or practices under §106.44(f)(1) through prompt and effective steps to end discrimination, prevent recurrence, and remedy effects, rather than via informal resolution between parties.
